headline: Connecticut colleges reported more than 100 rapes in 2025, campus data shows
dek: New Clery reports show wide differences among Connecticut campuses, but the figures count reports rather than proven crimes and cannot be used as a simple safety ranking.
body: Connecticut colleges and universities recorded more than 100 reports of rape in calendar year 2025, according to a review of newly released campus security reports. The figures span incidents reported to schools, campus security authorities, police and other designated officials, and they cover campus property, some school-controlled locations away from campus and certain nearby public areas. They are a record of reports, not a statewide count of prosecutions or a finding that every reported allegation was substantiated.

The numbers were compiled in an Oct. 7 [CT Insider review](https://www.ctinsider.com/news/education/article/campus-crime-reports-rape-ct-universities-2025-22462715.php) of annual security reports required under the federal Jeanne Clery Disclosure of Campus Security Policy and Campus Crime Statistics Act. The reports are released each year by colleges that participate in federal student-aid programs. The law is intended to make campus crime and safety information public, but its categories and geography are narrower than a general measure of all sexual violence affecting students.

A small group of schools accounted for much of the total. CT Insider’s compilation lists 37 reported rapes at the University of Hartford, 27 at Yale University and 13 at Trinity College. It lists six each at Connecticut College, the University of New Haven and Eastern Connecticut State University, with smaller totals at several other institutions. Yale’s reports were all categorized as occurring in student dormitories or other residential facilities. The Yale total rose from 19 in 2024 but remained below the 56 reported in 2023, according to the university’s report as summarized by CT Insider.

The University of Hartford’s [2026 Annual Security and Fire Safety Report](https://www.hartford.edu/student-life/public-safety/_files/2026-uhartford-annual-security-and-fire-report-final-9.30.2026.pdf) records 37 rape reports for 2025, including 36 in student housing. The report says a significant number resulted from one report and that an outside investigation found insufficient information to proceed. That explanation does not erase the report from the Clery count, but it does show why a high number cannot by itself establish how many separate assaults occurred or compare one campus fairly with another.

The University of Connecticut provides another example of why the data needs context. In its [release about the 2025 Clery report](https://today.uconn.edu/2026/09/uconn-releases-annual-safety-reports-8/), UConn says its count includes information from more than 1,200 campus security authorities, such as resident assistants, coaches and faculty advisers. The university also says it records reports even when details are incomplete or a third party makes the disclosure. CT Insider’s review lists three reported rapes at UConn’s Storrs campus, while UConn’s release describes two sexual-assault reports there, a difference that underscores how category labels and reporting rules can affect comparisons.

Other campuses reported few or no rapes in the same year. CT Insider lists no reported rapes at Wesleyan University or Quinnipiac University, while Southern Connecticut State University, Central Connecticut State University and Western Connecticut State University each reported one or two. Those figures should not be read as proof that no sexual violence occurred. The [Connecticut Alliance to End Sexual Violence](https://endsexualviolencect.org/) told CT Insider that Clery reports are a limited snapshot because many survivors do not report, and different campuses may have different levels of awareness, trust and access to reporting channels.

A separate [WFSB report](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/05/yales-sexual-violence-reports-far-exceed-other-ct-schools-police-point-location/) found that Yale’s numbers were much higher than those at most Connecticut schools and quoted New Haven police pointing to the university’s location near a midsize city as one factor that may influence reports. That is a possible explanation, not a conclusion about any individual case or campus. The Clery reports do not supply enough information to determine why one school’s numbers differ from another’s.

For students and families, the practical value of the reports is transparency rather than a league table. They identify what schools were told, where reports were categorized and what prevention, response and support policies campuses say they maintain. The next useful questions are whether students know how to report, whether confidential and non-police options are available, how institutions explain unusual statistical changes and what resources are offered regardless of whether a complainant seeks an investigation. The 2025 data makes those questions more visible across Connecticut, but it does not answer them on its own.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Connecticut colleges reported more than 100 rapes in 2025
seoDescription: New Clery reports show more than 100 rape reports at Connecticut colleges in 2025, with wide differences and important limits on comparison.
